studies.title: A Guide For Those Who Do Good
studies.meaning: The opening does not describe the Book to everyone. It calls the Book wise, then narrows the benefit: a guide and a mercy for those who do good. The next ayah defines that group by three things. They keep up the prayer, they give, and they hold the Hereafter as certain rather than probable. Guidance is then spoken of as something already possessed rather than promised, and success is stated as fact. The passage sorts its own audience before it says anything else.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period when the Quran was being publicly recited and publicly refused. This surah opens the way surahs 29, 30 and 32 open, with the same three disconnected letters, and the four stand together in the order of the Book. The classical commentators report no specific occasion for these ayat. They read them as the standard opening move of a Meccan surah: naming the Book, then naming who will benefit from it.

keyTerms.note: From a root covering both wisdom and a judge's authority to settle a matter. Applied to a book it suggests writing that is not merely intelligent but decided, holding its verdicts firmly in place.

The active form of a verb meaning to do something beautifully. It reaches past correctness to quality of execution, so it names people who do the right thing well rather than people who merely avoid wrong.
A verb of settled certainty rather than belief or opinion. It marks the Hereafter as something these people treat as established fact, which is a stronger claim than saying they hope it is true.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on recited speech. Poets were judged in public, verses were memorised by traders and carried along the caravan routes, and a striking line could reach Yemen or Syria within a season. A text announcing itself as a book, in a town where almost nothing was written down, was making an unusual claim. Listeners expecting a poem were handed something that behaved more like a register.
studies.didYouKnow: The three letters that open this surah open exactly six surahs in the Quran, and four of those six stand consecutively at 29, 30, 31 and 32. The phrase used here for the Book, rendered the Wise Book, occurs in only one other place in the whole Quran, at the head of surah 10.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is called guidance and mercy at once, which refuses any split between instruction and kindness. But it is guidance for a specified group, so the passage locates the variable in the receiver rather than in the text. Nothing here says the Book fails to reach anyone. It says the benefit lands where prayer, giving, and certainty about what comes after are already at work.

crossReferences.why: Opens the longest surah with the same move, naming the Book as guidance for those conscious of God.
The only other place that calls the revelation the Wise Book, again at the head of a surah.
States the other side: the same recitation is guidance and healing for some and obscurity for others.

studies.applyIt: Notice which of the three marks named here is weakest in you this week. Most people find it is the third, certainty about what comes after, because it never appears on a calendar. Give it five minutes tonight. Not an argument for it, just five minutes of sitting with the fact that you will one day be somewhere else.

studies.title: The Man Who Buys Distraction
studies.meaning: A single figure is described by what he purchases. He buys diverting talk and uses it to pull people off the road, and two further things are said about him: he does it without knowledge, and he treats the whole matter as a joke. The classical commentators differ over what the diverting talk is, listing song, storytelling, and imported legends set against the recitation, and the older sources record that range rather than fixing it. What is fixed is the purpose, not the medium.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report that some opponents met the recitation not with argument but with entertainment, bringing back tales from the northern trade routes and telling them in competing gatherings to draw listeners away. The reports describe the practice more confidently than they identify individuals, and most commentators read the ayah as naming a pattern rather than settling on one man in Mecca.

keyTerms.note: A commercial verb. It makes the distraction something acquired at a cost, which is how the ayah frames the choice: he spent something in order to obtain what leads away from the road.
Covers whatever occupies attention without feeding it, from play to entertainment. Its force here is not that the thing is wicked but that it is built to absorb, and absorption is the point.
The ayah adds ridicule on top of distraction. Turning something into a joke removes the need to answer it, which is a cheaper response than argument and frequently a more effective one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's evenings belonged to storytellers. A caravan returning from the Persian frontier brought goods and also tales of kings and champions, and a man with a good repertoire could hold a courtyard until late. Competing gatherings were an ordinary form of pressure in a town that small. You did not need to refute a speaker; you only needed to draw his listeners across the square to a better show.
studies.didYouKnow: The expression translated here as distracting tales occurs exactly once in the entire Quran, in this ayah. Because it appears nowhere else, the classical commentators had no internal parallel to fix its sense, and their readings spread accordingly, from song to imported foreign legends to any speech deployed to crowd out the recitation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The opposition described is not intellectual. Nothing is refuted here; attention is simply purchased elsewhere, and the ayah calls that leading people off the road. It treats what a person listens to as a matter with moral weight, and it identifies mockery as a technique rather than a conclusion. The judgement named is humiliation, which answers ridicule in its own currency.

crossReferences.why: The next ayah completes the portrait, showing the same man turning away in pride when the verses reach him.
Describes people who take their religion as play and pastime, using the same vocabulary of diversion.
Pairs hearing the verses recited with persisting in pride and taking them as a joke.

studies.applyIt: Look at what actually filled the last hour you meant to give to something else. You do not need to call it wrong. Just name what it was, and notice whether you chose it or it arrived. The word this ayah uses is a purchase, and a purchase has a price you can usually work out if you ask.

studies.title: As Though He Did Not Hear
studies.meaning: The refusal is described in stages. He hears, he turns away, and the turning is done in pride. Then two comparisons are laid on top, and both are hypothetical: as though he had not heard it, as though there were a weight in his ears. The passage never says his hearing failed. It says he behaves exactly as a deaf man would while hearing perfectly well, which puts the obstruction somewhere other than the ear. The closing instruction is bitter: announce good news of pain.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing the portrait begun in the ayah before. The recitation was public and hard to avoid in a small town built around a single shrine, so opponents could not simply miss it. The sources describe deliberate strategies for not hearing, including leaving gatherings and raising noise over the reciter. The commentators report no particular occasion, reading the ayah as a description of that behaviour.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to make oneself great rather than to be great. It presents pride as effort the person puts in, which is why it can be described as something done while turning, like a posture.
A weight in the ear rather than an absence of hearing. The image is of something loaded on top of a working faculty, which is why the ayah can apply it to a man who plainly did hear.

The verb belongs to glad tidings and is used almost everywhere else for reward. Attaching it to punishment is deliberate, and Arabic rhetoric recognises the reversal as a recognised form of sharp irony.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The courtyard around the Kaaba was the town's public room. Business, judgement, poetry and pilgrimage happened in the same space, and a man reciting there could not be avoided by anyone doing ordinary business. Not hearing in Mecca took work: choosing another route, arriving later, keeping a conversation loud on the way past. The image of stopped ears would have read as a description of effort, not of disability.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of a weight in the ears appears in six ayat of the Quran and never once describes a physical condition. Five times it is God's diagnosis of people refusing a message. In the sixth, opponents say it about themselves as a boast, telling the Prophet that their ears are already stopped against whatever he is calling them to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hearing is treated as insufficient on its own. The passage separates reception from response and puts the failure in the will, which preserves both the clarity of the message and the responsibility of the listener. It also refuses to let pride stay private: arrogance is shown as a bodily act, a turn of the shoulder performed in public. Nothing is said here about capacity, only about what was done with it.

crossReferences.why: The opponents describe themselves in the same terms, claiming their own ears are already stopped.
Compares calling those who refuse to shouting at animals that catch the sound but not the meaning.
Describes people with ears that do not hear, locating the fault in the heart rather than the organ.

studies.applyIt: Think of one piece of advice you have heard more than three times and still have not acted on. You did hear it. Say out loud, once, what it was and who said it to you. Naming it removes the option of pretending it never arrived, and that pretence is the whole distance this ayah is describing.

studies.title: A Promise Stated As Fact
studies.meaning: After two ayat of portraiture on refusal, the sentence turns and stays short. Belief and good deeds are named together, the reward is named, and the permanence is added as its own clause rather than folded in. Then something unusual happens. The promise is called true, and two names close the passage: might and wisdom. The reward is not left standing as an assurance about the future. It is grounded in what the one making the promise is like.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a stretch when the community was small and materially worse off than the people refusing the message. Assurances about the Hereafter carried the weight in this period that legislation would carry later in Medina. The commentators read the placement as structural rather than occasioned: the surah has just described a punishment of humiliation, and this restores the balance by naming the other outcome immediately instead of saving it for the end.

keyTerms.note: An intensive from a root for ease and comfortable living. It names the quality of the gardens rather than their contents, so the phrase describes what being there is like rather than what is in it.
The root carries long continuance rather than strict eternity in ordinary Arabic usage. The Quran attaches it to the final abode, where the commentators take the sense as settled and without end.
Placed in a case that reads as an emphatic aside rather than as part of the clause, roughly a promise from God, binding upon Him. The grammar makes the guarantee an interjection into the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing in Mecca lasted. Wells silted, wealth passed with a bad season, an alliance held only as long as the men who swore it were alive, and the town's own prosperity rode on trade routes that could move. Permanence was not a familiar category there. A garden that does not end was strange in a way modern readers miss: the surprising word in the phrase was not garden but forever.
studies.didYouKnow: The plural phrase rendered Gardens of Bliss occurs in seven ayat of the Quran, spread across seven different surahs. A singular form, one Garden of Bliss, occurs in only two places, and both sit inside speech rather than description: one in a prayer of Abraham, the other in a question put to people who expect to be admitted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two names close the passage, and the pairing does real work. Might alone would make the promise a matter of raw power; wisdom alone would make it a matter of good intention. Together they answer the two separate doubts a person actually has, whether the promiser can deliver and whether he can be trusted with the delivery. Hope is grounded in the character of the promiser, not in the appeal of the thing promised.

crossReferences.why: Names the opposite outcome, a humiliating punishment, in the same compact form two ayat earlier.
Uses the same emphatic phrase, calling God's promise true, then asks whose word could be truer.
Adds that those in the gardens will not wish to be moved from them to anywhere else.

studies.applyIt: Pick one small good thing you do that nobody notices. A message you send, a bill you quietly cover, a job you finish properly when nobody would check. Do it once this week without mentioning it to anyone. These ayat name belief and deeds in the same breath, and this is the cheapest way to keep them in the same breath in your own life.

studies.title: Pillars You Cannot See
studies.meaning: Four acts arrive in one breath: the heavens raised, weights set on the earth so it does not lurch, creatures scattered across it, water sent down and pairs made to grow. The clause about pillars is read two ways in the classical sources. Either there are no pillars at all, or there are pillars you cannot see, and the older commentators record both without deciding between them. Either reading leaves the same point standing. Something is holding, and nothing visible is doing the holding.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and placed immediately before a direct challenge: now show me what those besides Him have created. At this stage the surah is arguing from workmanship rather than from scripture, addressed to people who did not deny that God made the world and who worshipped intermediaries alongside Him. The commentators treat the sequence as a single case built for that audience rather than as a reply to any particular event.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a ship dropping anchor and holding fast. It is not the ordinary word for a mountain; it names a function, so the emphasis falls on holding steady rather than on height.
The verb used of a tilting ship or a person losing footing. It gives the earth a motion the passage then says has been prevented, which is why the anchor image was reached for.
The word for one of a couple, used here of plants. It builds pairing into growing things themselves, so the vegetation is described in the same terms as living creatures rather than as scenery.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An Arabian caravan navigated by landmarks: a particular ridge, a black hill, a line of peaks telling a guide he was two days from water. Mountains were not scenery but fixed points in a country where everything else moved. Sand shifted, wells failed, camps broke and re-formed. The word used here for those anchors comes from the sea, and Meccan traders knew the Red Sea ports as well as they knew the ridges.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about heavens raised without pillars that you can see appears in exactly two places in the Quran, here and near the start of surah 13. In both it opens an argument about creation rather than closing one, and in both the Arabic leaves the same ambiguity that has kept the commentators from agreeing on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument runs on ordinary observation rather than on revelation, which makes it usable by someone who does not yet accept the Book. It also describes God's action as continuing rather than finished: the earth is being held, not merely made. That distinction carries weight, because a world made once and then left could be credited to a maker without granting Him any present claim on anyone.

crossReferences.why: The only other place speaking of heavens raised without pillars that you can see.
Repeats the anchoring of the earth and gives the same reason, lest it shift with you.
Puts the same image as a question, calling the earth a bed and the mountains pegs.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once this week at a time when you can see a long way, and find the highest fixed thing in view. Look at it for a full minute without doing anything else. The ayah is asking for this and nothing more: that you notice something is holding, and that you had no hand in putting it there.

studies.title: Wisdom Given As Gratitude
studies.meaning: A challenge is issued and then an example is produced. The challenge is empirical rather than doctrinal: point to anything the other objects of devotion have made. Then a sage is introduced, and what he was given is named as wisdom and immediately explained by a single instruction, to give thanks. The commentators notice that when the content of the wisdom is finally stated it is neither a doctrine nor a technique but a disposition. The closing clause keeps the whole benefit on the human side.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Luqman was already a proverbial figure in Arabia, quoted for his sayings the way a familiar sage is quoted anywhere. The Quran does not call him a prophet, and the classical commentators generally treat him as a wise man rather than a messenger; their reports about his origins differ, most often describing him as Abyssinian or Nubian. Taking a respected outsider as the surah's teacher was itself a choice.

keyTerms.note: From the root of the bridle that restrains a horse. Wisdom in Arabic is first the capacity to hold back and steer, which is why it names judgement in action rather than knowledge stored.
A command to produce something visible, not to argue. It asks for an exhibit, which is why the challenge that follows cannot be answered by an appeal to what people have always assumed.
A form meaning praised and deserving praise at once. Placed after ingratitude is mentioned, it says the praise is owed by the nature of the thing, whether or not anyone offers it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wisdom travelled orally and by name. Sayings were carried between Yemen, Syria and Mecca with the caravans, quoted at gatherings, and attributed to the men who first said them, and a reputation for good judgement was a genuine asset in a society that arbitrated disputes by respected elders. Luqman's sayings were in circulation in Arabia before this surah gave him a chapter.
studies.didYouKnow: Luqman is one of very few people the Quran names who is not presented as a prophet, and the surah carries his name although he appears in only a handful of its thirty-four ayat. His speech occupies a short stretch in the middle, and the surah returns to argument about creation on either side of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Wisdom is defined by the first thing it produces, and that turns out to be thankfulness rather than insight. The definition places the crown of intelligence in an orientation toward the giver rather than in information held. The divine name that closes the passage then separates God's worth from human acknowledgement entirely, which is what makes gratitude a benefit received rather than a duty owed to someone in need of it.

crossReferences.why: States what is being handed over here: whoever is given wisdom has been given a great deal of good.
Closes with almost the same formula, gratitude credited to the grateful and God free of need.
Supplies the promise attached to thankfulness that this passage assumes without repeating.

studies.applyIt: Think of the most level-headed person you know personally, the one whose judgement you would actually borrow. Over the next week, notice what they are thankful for and to whom they say so. The connection this passage makes between good judgement and gratitude is not obvious, and the easiest place to test it is in someone you can watch.

studies.title: A Father Advises His Son
studies.meaning: A father's counsel, arranged from the largest matter to the smallest without a break between them. It begins with not associating anything with God, and it ends with how loudly to speak. In between come prayer, calling to what is right, patience with what lands on you, and the way a person holds their face in company. Two ayat in the middle are not the father's words at all. They interrupt in another voice to speak about parents, including the case where parents press their own child in the opposite direction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. In Mecca the sharpest cost of accepting the message was domestic: parents disowned children, and households divided along a line nobody had chosen. The inserted ayat address exactly that pressure, and they are careful about it, setting a limit on obedience in one respect while leaving the relationship itself intact. Putting the counsel in the mouth of a sage the audience already respected gave it a hearing before the argument began.

keyTerms.note: A loss of strength rather than an ache. Repeating it describes a weakness laid on top of an existing weakness, which is how the ayah renders the months of carrying a child.
The known and acknowledged, the same word used for right conduct generally. Companionship on those terms means the ordinary decency any community would recognise, owed regardless of the disagreement.
A joy that spills into display. It names the pleased self-importance in a way of walking, not happiness itself, which is why the counsel that follows is about stride and volume.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bearing was read closely in that society. Turning the cheek away from someone was a recognised snub, and a man's stride and the pitch of his voice in a crowded market announced how he wished to be taken. Children were carried on the hip through moves between pasture and settlement, and weaning at around two years was ordinary. The comparison at the end uses the loudest animal anybody worked with.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of these seven ayat are not spoken by the father at all. After the first line of advice, the voice changes to speak about parents in general and about the limit of what they may ask, and then the original address resumes with the same words it used before. The counsel is interrupted from outside and then handed back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The gravest matter and one of the smallest sit inside a single continuous counsel: what a person worships, and how loudly they talk. That treats character as one fabric rather than as separate departments of belief and manners. The interruption about parents establishes something else, that a duty can be limited in one direction and unlimited in another, and that a disagreement about the largest question does not cancel the ordinary decencies.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction about parents with the image of lowering the wing of humility over them.
Repeats the detail of carrying and weaning, and turns it into a prayer offered at forty.
Describes the same bearing from the other side, servants of the Merciful who walk the earth gently.

studies.applyIt: Call whoever raised you, or the person who stood closest to that role, and ask one question about their own parents that you have never asked. Not about you, and not about the present. Then let them talk. This passage puts the debt to parents in terms of what they carried before you could remember any of it.

studies.title: Blessings Outward And Inward
studies.meaning: The question is put to everyone: everything above and below has been set to work for you, and the favours poured over you come in two kinds, the ones you can see and the ones you cannot. The classical commentators fill out the hidden column with health, understanding, faith, and every harm quietly kept away. Then the sentence turns without warning to a man who argues about God with three things missing. No knowledge, no guidance, and no book that gives light.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been building its case from creation, and this ayah restates the case in the second person before naming the kind of opponent it has in view. The commentators report no specific occasion. They observe that the three things the arguer lacks correspond to the three ordinary grounds for any claim in that setting: what you have worked out, what you were shown, and what you can produce in writing.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of harnessing an animal or compelling a servant to a task. Applied to the heavens and the earth it describes them as put at human disposal without being handed over in ownership.
From a root describing a coat of mail hanging long enough to cover completely. The image is of a covering that extends past what is strictly needed, which is why translators reach for showered.
The counterpart of what is outward. Used of favours it covers everything that never registers as a gift: an illness that did not arrive, a decision quietly kept from going wrong.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan household counted its blessings in visible things. Camels, a share in a caravan, sons, a place in the shade near the Kaaba. Nothing in that ledger counted what had not happened: the raid that passed down the next valley, the fever that broke, the well that did not run dry that year. This ayah adds a second column to an account book everyone in the town kept carefully in one.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of outward and inward favours occurs exactly once in the Quran, in this ayah. Both words are used elsewhere in the Book, but never together of blessings, so the phrase has no internal parallel to fix its range. The classical lists of what counts as an inward favour vary considerably as a result.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes ingratitude a failure of knowing as well as a failure of character. It names three sources of warranted claim and says the arguer holds none of them, which sets a standard for speech about God that applies to anyone who speaks about Him. And by naming hidden favours it makes gratitude something that can never be completed, since the full list is not available to the one being grateful.

crossReferences.why: Names the identical three lacks in a man who argues about God: knowledge, guidance, and an illuminating book.
States the other half: if you tried to count God's favours you could not number them.
Uses the same verb for everything in the heavens and the earth being set to work for human beings.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, write down two things that did not happen to you today. A near miss in traffic, a message that could have gone badly and did not, a pain you braced for and never got. They will feel like nothing, which is exactly the point. This ayah says roughly half of what you have been given sits in that column.

studies.title: What We Found Our Fathers On
studies.meaning: A short exchange. They are told to follow what God sent down, and they answer with what they inherited. The reply is not an argument against the message; it is a refusal to weigh it at all. The Quran answers with a question rather than a refutation: would they follow even if the one calling them were Satan and the destination the fire. The force of the question is that inheritance says nothing about direction. A thing can be old, widely held, and yours by birth, and still be going somewhere.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Ancestral practice was the central defence of Meccan religion, and the Quran quotes that defence in almost identical words in four separate places, put in the mouths of different peoples in different eras. Placed here, directly after a passage about arguing without knowledge, guidance or a book, it shows what people reach for once those three grounds have been ruled out.

keyTerms.note: Broader than fathers. It reaches back to ancestors and to the line as a whole, which is what gives the answer its weight in a society organised entirely around descent.
The verb for walking behind someone on a road. Both sides of the exchange use it, so the disagreement is not over whether to follow but over whom, which is what the closing question presses.
A particle opening a hypothetical the speaker has not considered. It does not deny that the ancestors existed or were loved. It asks whether the fact of them settles anything at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Mecca a man's standing was his lineage, recited aloud and defended in verse. Trade partnerships, marriage, blood money and protection all ran through descent. To break with what your fathers did was to loosen the only rope holding you to a place. The message was not asking for a change of opinion. It was asking men to risk the structure that fed them and defended them.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence the opponents speak here, that they follow what they found their fathers upon, appears in exactly this form in four ayat of the Quran, in surahs 5, 7, 10 and 31, spoken each time by a different group in a different century. The Book treats it less as an argument than as a recurring reflex.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the truth of a claim from the route by which it reached you. Inheritance is not condemned; it is denied the standing of evidence. That leaves the reader with something uncomfortable, since most of what anyone believes did in fact arrive by inheritance, and the ayah asks only that the arrival not be mistaken for a reason to keep it.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same reply and answers it directly, asking what if their fathers understood nothing at all.
Shows the response is not local: every warned town before Mecca gave a version of the same answer.
Records the reply being used to defend an indecency, showing how far the reflex can stretch.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you believe strongly that you have never actually examined, and be honest that you hold it because the people who raised you held it. You do not have to change it. Just move it, for one week, from the shelf marked settled to the shelf marked inherited, and see whether it looks different sitting there.

studies.title: The Most Trustworthy Handle
studies.meaning: Two conditions are named, then one image. A person turns his face wholly toward God and does good, and the result is described as taking hold of a grip that will not give way. The metaphor is physical, and it is not about being carried. It is about gripping. Submission and doing good are put together so that neither can stand alone. The closing clause then moves the outcome of every matter away from the one holding on, and sets it where the handle is fixed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just quoted people who follow inherited practice, and this ayah names the alternative in a single sentence, without argument. The classical commentators note that the same handhold image appears once more in the Quran, in a Medinan passage about compulsion in religion, and read both as describing a deliberate act of taking hold rather than a state anyone drifts into.

keyTerms.note: The face stands for the whole person and for what he turns toward. Surrendering it means orientation rather than opinion: which way you are facing when nobody is directing you.
The loop on a bucket, a waterskin or a garment, the part made to be held. It names something designed for gripping, so the image implies a handle that was provided rather than found.
A superlative from a root for binding fast, which also gives the word for a solemn covenant. The handle therefore carries an overtone of something guaranteed rather than merely strong.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world moved by rope and loop. Waterskins hung from a loop at the saddle, buckets went down wells on plaited cord, and loads were lashed to a camel's frame by hand before dawn. Every traveller knew the specific fear of a strap parting over open ground. Choosing a good handle was a daily judgement with real consequences, and the metaphor needed no explanation at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as the most trustworthy handle occurs exactly twice in the Quran: here, and in the Medinan ayah that says there is no compulsion in religion. One is Meccan and one Medinan, and in both the gripping is something the person does, never something done to him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is presented as an act with an object rather than as a feeling. The image supplies both the security and its limit, since a handle holds only while it is held. And pairing inward surrender with visible good refuses to let orientation certify itself: the ayah names a second condition, observable to others, alongside the first one, which is not.

crossReferences.why: The only other place using this handhold image, immediately after saying there is no compulsion in religion.
Uses the same phrase about surrendering the face to God, and adds doing good in the same breath.
Turns the image outward, telling a whole community to hold fast together to the rope of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you are currently holding on to for security. A job, a saved amount, a particular person's approval. Do not let go of it. Just ask honestly what would happen if it gave way, and whether there is anything underneath it. That question is the entire content of this ayah, and it is better asked on a calm day.

studies.title: Let His Refusal Not Grieve You
studies.meaning: The instruction is not given to the one refusing but to the one watching him. Grief at another person's choice is addressed directly and then set aside, and the reason offered is jurisdiction. Their return is to Us, their record will be read to them by Us, and God knows what is inside chests. After that the timing is supplied. There is a short enjoyment and then a compulsion toward something heavy. Nothing is said about changing the person. The passage is about where the weight of his choice belongs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a stretch when the message was being publicly refused by men the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had grown up among and knew personally. Several passages from this period address his distress directly, which the classical commentators take as a measure of how heavily it pressed. No specific occasion is reported for these two ayat; they belong to the closing argument of the surah rather than to any single incident.

keyTerms.note: The verb of sorrow rather than anger or worry. The construction addresses the grief itself instead of forbidding an action, which treats the feeling as the thing being adjusted here.
An idiom for the innermost contents of a person, closer to what someone is than to what they think. It puts the judgement beyond anything an observer could reasonably assess.
From a root for necessity and being forced by circumstance. The same root gives the word for a person driven by desperation, so the verb carries the sense of leaving no alternative open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small enough that refusal came from relatives. Uncles, cousins, business partners and childhood companions stood on the other side of the argument, and there was no avoiding them at the well, in the market, or during the pilgrimage season. Grief over another person's choice was not an abstraction in that town. It arrived at meals, and it sat down.
studies.didYouKnow: The expression for what lies within the chests occurs twelve times in the Quran, and in nearly every case it closes an ayah rather than opening one. It works as a formula for ending a discussion of human motive, which is precisely its function here, where another person's inner state is being taken out of the reader's hands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line around responsibility. Conveying is one thing and outcome is another, and the grief that comes from confusing the two is named and addressed rather than admired. It also refuses to let that boundary harden into indifference: mentioning a short comfort followed by something heavy keeps the stakes entirely real while lifting the burden of enforcing them.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether he will destroy himself with grief over those who will not believe this message.
Repeats the instruction almost exactly, telling him not to waste himself away in sorrow over them.
States the limit plainly: he was not appointed as a guardian or a keeper over them.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose choices you have been carrying. Write one sentence saying what you have actually said to them, and one sentence saying what is now out of your hands. Then leave the second sentence alone for a week. This ayah is not asking you to stop caring. It is asking you to stop auditing.

studies.title: They Will Certainly Say, God
studies.meaning: A test question is posed with the answer supplied in advance. Ask them who made the heavens and the earth, and they will say God. The Quran does not treat that as a victory. The response commanded is praise, followed by a flat statement that most of them do not know, which means the admission and the knowing are two different things. The next ayah supplies what the admission failed to carry. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and He needs nothing from any of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people addressed were not atheists. They acknowledged a supreme creator and worshipped intermediaries they believed would bring them closer to Him. Several passages from this period use the same technique of quoting the opponents' own theology back to them. The commentators read the sequence as showing that the disagreement was never about whether God exists, but about what follows once you have said so.

keyTerms.note: Carries a double emphasis in Arabic, an oath particle in front and a heavy ending behind. The Quran is not guessing at their answer here; it commits to that answer in advance.
From a root meaning to have no need. Applied to God it removes exchange from worship altogether, since nothing offered supplies a lack, which changes what an act of devotion is for.
The form covers both being praised and deserving praise. Paired with self-sufficiency it means praise adds nothing to Him, which places the entire benefit on the side of the one praising.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan religion was transactional in a perfectly ordinary way. Offerings went to the shrine, shares of crops and livestock were assigned to particular deities, and the arrangement worked like the patronage everyone knew from trade. You gave to someone above you and expected protection in return. A God described as needing nothing did not improve the terms of that arrangement. It broke the model.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of the two names that closes this passage occurs five times in the Quran, and in four of those five it follows either a statement about who owns the heavens and the earth or a statement about people turning away. The combination reads almost as a closing formula rather than as a description offered on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates belief in a creator from religion. Assent to the bare fact turns out to be compatible with not knowing, which places knowledge somewhere other than in propositions a person holds. The two names that close it then remove the transactional frame entirely. If God gains nothing, worship cannot be a payment, and its whole purpose has to be relocated to the worshipper.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical question about the sun and moon and predicts the identical answer from the same people.
Quotes their own stated reason for the intermediaries: only to bring us nearer to God.
States the other side of self-sufficiency directly: it is you who are the poor, needing God.

studies.applyIt: Sometime today you will say something true about God almost automatically, in a greeting, in a word of thanks, after bad news. When you catch it happening, stop for three seconds and ask whether you meant it or simply said it. The entire weight of this ayah sits in the gap between those two, and the gap opens only when you notice.

studies.title: If Every Tree Were Pens
studies.meaning: Two scales are set side by side and the pairing is the point. First an inventory of the whole world as writing equipment: every tree cut into pens, the sea as ink with seven more behind it, and still the words of God would not run out. The commentators read those words as His knowledge and His acts of command rather than as a text with a page count. Then the direction reverses. Making and raising all of humanity is described as no more than doing it for one person.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage follows the observation that if the objectors were asked who made the heavens and the earth they would answer God, and would then carry on as before. So the argument is not aimed at people who deny a maker. It works instead on the size of what they had already conceded, and on the assumption hidden inside their behaviour, that a very great act must cost a very great effort.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a reed trimmed to a nib. Writing tools were made by hand from a specific plant, so imagining every tree as pens counts a scarce resource rather than reaching for a poetic flourish.
Not sentences on a page. The Quran uses this plural for God's decrees and effective speech, so what cannot be exhausted is the acting and knowing rather than a quantity of text.
In Arabic usage the number regularly stands for an indefinite multitude rather than a count, which is why the image is not asking the listener to picture exactly seven additional bodies of water.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing was expensive and slow. Ink was mixed from soot and gum, pens were cut from reeds and trimmed as they wore, and text went onto parchment, palm stalks, flat stones and shoulder blades because sheets were costly. Scribes were specialists whose services were hired. An audience that knew what a single letter cost would hear this image as an accounting problem.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives this picture twice, with different quantities. In Surah 18, at ayah one hundred and nine, the sea itself would be exhausted as ink before the words of the Lord were exhausted, even with another sea like it brought in. Here the sea is multiplied further and every tree is added, and the conclusion is unchanged.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Set together, the two ayat say something neither could say alone. Inexhaustibility is asserted and effort is denied in consecutive sentences, which blocks the inference a listener would otherwise draw, that an act on that scale must be a strain. The closing names then bring the scale back to the person being addressed: the one for whom all of humanity is as one soul is also hearing and seeing them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same image with a smaller quantity of ink and the identical conclusion about words not running out.
States the cost of a divine act directly: the command is a single word said to a thing.
Puts the same point in terms of time, one command, no slower than the blink of an eye.

studies.applyIt: Take the one thing you carry that seems too large to hand over, the situation you have decided is beyond anyone's fixing. Say it out loud in a single sentence, addressed to God, without adding a request. The second of these two ayat is about scale: what is enormous to you is not a different order of task for the one you are speaking to.

studies.title: Each Running To A Term
studies.meaning: Two motions are described in one sentence and they belong to different scales. The night is fed into the day and the day into the night, a merging with no visible seam, and the sun and moon are set running to an appointed end. Then the ayah closes somewhere unexpected. God is aware of what you do. A passage about the movement of the heavens ends on human conduct, which turns the astronomy into an argument about being watched rather than an argument about design.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, part of the closing sequence of signs in this surah. The verb used for merging night into day appears in only four places in the Quran, and each of them makes the same point about a change too gradual to catch as it happens. The commentators report no occasion for this ayah, reading it as one of several appeals to what any listener could confirm by standing outside at dusk.

keyTerms.note: From a root for entering and being let in. The verb makes the transition an act of insertion rather than a replacement, so night is described as fed into day rather than as following it.
The Quran's standard phrase for a limit already fixed and named. Applied to the sun and moon it puts an expiry date on the two things a seventh-century listener would call permanent.
From a root for knowing something by testing and probing it. It suggests inside knowledge gained through examination rather than observation from a distance, which is why it lands at the end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian life was calibrated to exactly this merging. Travel started before first light and stopped when the heat made it impossible, prayers and market hours were read off the sun's position, and a caravan crossing open country steered by stars for half of every night. Nobody in that audience needed the phenomenon explained. What was new was the claim that one hand ran both the schedule and the conduct.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for merging night into day occurs in only four ayat of the Quran, and in every one of them it is doubled, night into day and then day into night, so the reciprocal shape is never broken. Three of those four close on a statement about what God hears, sees or knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places continuous divine action in the most regular setting available. Nothing here is a miracle or an interruption; the whole argument runs on what happens every single day, which makes reliability rather than spectacle the evidence being offered. Attaching an appointed term to the sun and moon does further work. It denies permanence to the largest visible things, and so denies them any claim on worship.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same doubled verb and closes on God knowing what the chests contain.
Expands the appointed courses of sun and moon, adding that neither one overtakes the other.
Names the alternation of night and day as a sign for people who actually think about it.

studies.applyIt: Watch one sunset this week from beginning to end, without a screen in your hand. You will find you cannot identify the moment it becomes night, and that missing seam is exactly what the verb in this ayah describes. Ten minutes is enough. Then notice that the last thing the ayah mentions is not the sky but what you did today.

studies.title: Signs For Every Thankful One
studies.meaning: Two statements are joined here. The first is a verdict on reality: God is the Real, and what they call on beside Him is the void, with two names following, high and great. The second is a scene, ships moving across water by God's favour so that He may show you His signs. Then the audience narrows sharply. The signs are said to be there for every person who is much-enduring and much-thanking, which makes reading the world a matter of character rather than of intelligence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca did not sit on the sea, but its wealth came from caravans feeding the Red Sea ports, so shipping was a familiar image rather than an exotic one. The commentators treat these two ayat as the pivot into the surah's final sequence, where the argument shifts from what God made to what happens inside a person in danger, which the following ayah takes up at once.

keyTerms.note: A word covering truth, reality and rightful claim at once. Used as a name it says God is what is actually there, which is why its opposite in the same sentence is emptiness rather than error.
From a root for something null, cancelled, without content. It is a heavier charge than untrue: what is described is not a mistaken belief but an object with nothing inside it.
Both are intensive forms, naming habits rather than single acts. Paired, they cover the two halves of any life, what is hard and what is given, and the signs are legible to someone practised at both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Red Sea was a shallow, reef-scattered, difficult water that traders used anyway, because the alternative was months overland. Ships worked the coast from Jeddah and Ayla with cargo that finished its journey by camel. A Meccan merchant did not sail himself, but he knew men who did, knew what a lost cargo did to a season, and knew that a hull holding together over deep water was not a thing to assume.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of intensive words that closes this passage occurs exactly four times in the Quran, always in this order and always naming who is able to read a sign. It appears in the charge given to Moses, here, in the account of Sheba, and after a passage about ships becalmed. Two of the four attach it to ships.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes perception a moral matter. Signs are described as present and public, and yet the ayah says they exist for a particular kind of person, which means the limiting factor is formation rather than evidence. The two qualities named are also the two available responses to the only two things that happen to anyone, hardship and gift. Reading the world rightly is presented as the by-product of having answered both properly.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same closing phrase of a becalmed ship, so the sign holds in stillness as well as motion.
Attaches the same pair to remembering the days of God, in the charge given to Moses.
States the same contrast in nearly identical words: God is the Real, what they invoke is void.

studies.applyIt: The next time something small goes right, the bus is there, the pain eases, a difficult message gets a kind reply, say thank you out loud before you move on. It takes two seconds. This ayah says signs become visible to people who have made a habit of exactly that, and the habit is built at this size and no other.

studies.title: When The Waves Cover Them
studies.meaning: A storm strips the theology bare. Waves rise over the ship like awnings and everyone aboard calls on God alone, with the religion made purely His, which is exactly the position the surah has been arguing toward. Then land arrives and the sincerity thins. The Arabic of what follows is compressed, and the commentators differ over whether it means some keep faith only partly or some hold a middle course between gratitude and denial. What is not in doubt is that the clarity of the storm did not survive the harbour.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is one of three passages in the Quran built on the same scene, and the repetition suggests something recognised rather than invented. The commentators attach no occasion to it. They do note its placement: it follows two ayat about ships as signs, so the same vessel that carried an argument about God's favour now carries an argument about human memory.

keyTerms.note: The word for shade structures, the stretched cloth roofs over a market stall or a tent. It gives the wave both its height and its overhang, arriving above you rather than merely against you.

From a root for something refined until nothing foreign remains in it. It describes worship with the additions stripped out, which is what the surah has been asking for and what the storm produces by force.
An intensive form for one who breaks a pledge repeatedly. It is rare in the Quran, and it frames the return to old habits as the breaking of a promise made out on the water.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Red Sea crews knew the storms by name and the reefs by feel, and a passage that should take days could take weeks. Vows made at sea were an ordinary institution across the ancient world: a merchant in danger promised an offering, a gift to a shrine, a share of the cargo. The pattern this ayah describes was not a moral hypothesis for its first listeners. It was a known feature of the shipping trade.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran tells this same scene three times, in surahs 10, 29 and here, with nearly identical wording for the prayer at the peak of the storm and a different ending each time. One closes with transgression on land, one with returning to other gods the moment they are safe, and this one with wavering.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies pure devotion as something already present in every person, surfaced by danger rather than taught by it. That is a claim about human nature: the monotheism the surah argues for is not being introduced but recovered. It also sets the harder problem, which is not whether people can be sincere but whether sincerity survives safety, and the ayah offers no comfortable answer to that.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same storm, with the vow at the peak of the wave and the forgetting once ashore.
Ends the same scene differently, with a return to associating partners the moment they reach land.
Adds that the same forgetting follows rescue from any distress, not only from danger at sea.

studies.applyIt: Remember the last time you were genuinely afraid and prayed like you meant it. What did you say you would do. You almost certainly did not do it, and this ayah is not written to shame you for that. It is written so that you notice the pattern. Pick the smallest piece of that promise and do it this week.

studies.title: No Parent Can Avail His Child
studies.meaning: The address widens to all people, and the day is described by the one thing it removes. A father cannot discharge anything on his son's behalf, and a son cannot discharge anything for his father. The mutual phrasing matters. The ayah says it in both directions, so nobody can read the first half and quietly assume the second. Then two warnings close it, and they are separate: do not let this life deceive you, and do not let the deceiver deceive you about God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the final address of a surah whose middle section is a father advising his son. The placement is deliberate. The counsel earlier in the surah is the most a parent can give, and this ayah names its limit. The commentators report no occasion for it, treating the ending as the surah's step back from a single household to everyone listening.

keyTerms.note: The verb for settling a debt or standing in for an obligation. It rules out substitution rather than help, so what is denied is one person's account being paid out of another's.

An intensive form for one who deceives repeatedly, read by the commentators as Satan and also more broadly as anything that flatters. The related verb has already appeared in the same ayah, of this life.
From a root for shielding oneself from harm. Taking God as its object produces awareness rather than fright: keeping something in view because of what it entails for you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An Arabian man's security was his kin. Blood money was paid by the clan, a debt could be assumed by a brother, a father's standing protected sons who had none of their own, and an outsider with no such network could be killed with little consequence. Substitution was the basic mechanism of that society, its insurance and its courtroom. This ayah names one day on which the mechanism is simply not available.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where the impossibility of standing in for another is stated in both directions inside a single sentence, parent for child and child for parent. Elsewhere the point is made about friends, intercessors, or wealth. The doubled family form appears here alone, closing the surah named for a father's advice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is made non-transferable, which was a hard claim in a world organised around collective liability, and the passage does not soften it. But it is set inside an address to all people rather than a warning aimed at a group. The two closing clauses then distinguish being fooled by life from being fooled about God, and the second is the more serious, since it outlives disillusionment with the first.

crossReferences.why: The father's counsel earlier in this surah is what a parent can give; this names what he cannot.
States the same limit in the language of intercession and compensation on the day of reckoning.
Extends it to the closest ties, with a man willing to ransom himself using his own children.

studies.applyIt: Sit with one parent or one child this week and say something you have been assuming they already know. This ayah is not a reason to care less about them. It is a reason to notice that whatever passes between you has to pass now, in words, while the transfer is still open to you.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: In What Land You Will Die
studies.meaning: Five items are named as belonging to God's knowledge, and the last two are placed inside the listener's own life: what you will earn tomorrow, and the ground you will be buried in. The commentators treat the list as marking the limits of human knowing rather than as an exhaustive catalogue of the unseen. The word chosen for rain is worth noticing too. It is not the general term but the one used of rain that arrives after people have given up on it, so even the weather is named as relief.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the closing ayah of the surah. The lines just before it warn against being deceived by this life and describe a day on which no parent will be of use to a child. Ending a surah about wisdom with a list of what nobody can know is a deliberate move: the chapter that opened by giving a man sound judgement closes by marking where judgement runs out and where knowledge stops.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for a portion of time, used with the article for the end of everything. Naming it so plainly keeps the event on the same scale as any other hour rather than inflating it.
A word for rain understood as rescue, related to the cry for help. It appears only a handful of times in the Quran and elsewhere describes rain sent after people have despaired of it.
The commercial verb for gain, applied to deeds throughout the Quran. Using it of tomorrow keeps both meanings live, the wage and the record, without separating them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: These were precisely the things Arabian society paid to have predicted. Diviners were consulted about whether the rains would come, about whether a pregnancy would produce a son, and about the right day to set out. Their fees were real and their answers were remembered. Dying far from home was a specific fear for men who travelled for months, since it meant burial among strangers who owed you nothing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for rain is not the Quran's usual one. It occurs only a few times in the whole text, and where it does the sense is consistent: rain that arrives after people have stopped expecting it, sent as relief. The list of things known only to God therefore includes one item named by its mercy rather than by its mechanism.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line rather than issuing a threat. Two of the five items sit inside the reader's own biography, which turns an abstract statement about divine knowledge into a description of the reader's condition: you do not know what tomorrow will pay you or what country your grave is in. That makes every plan provisional without making planning pointless, which is a narrower claim than fatalism.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same boundary at greater length, down to a leaf falling and a seed in the dark earth.
Draws the practical consequence for speech: never say of anything that you will do it tomorrow.
Uses the same word for relieving rain, sent down after people have already given up hope.

studies.applyIt: The next time you tell someone what you will be doing next month, add a short qualifier and mean it rather than saying it as a habit. Then notice how the sentence feels different. This ayah puts two items from your own future outside your knowledge, and speech is the first place that either shows or hides.
